Myasthenia gravis in a pediatric patient with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome following
responsive neurostimulation device implantation: illustrative case
David A. Zuckerman, MBE,1 Cameron P. Beaudreault, MS,1 Carrie R. Muh, MD,1,2 Patricia E. McGoldrick, NP, MPA, MSN,1,3,4 and
Steven M. Wolf, MD1,3,4
1
New York Medical College, Valhalla, New York; 2Department of Neurosurgery, Westchester Medical Center, Valhalla, New York; 3Department of Pediatrics, Division of Pediatric
Neurology, Maria Fareri Children’s Hospital, Valhalla, New York; and 4
Boston Children’s Hospital Physicians, Hawthorne, New York
BACKGROUND Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder in which the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor of the neuromuscular junction is
destroyed by autoantibodies. The authors report a case of MG in a pediatric patient who also suffered from Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS) and is
one of a limited number of pediatric patients who have undergone placement of a responsive neurostimulation (RNS) device (NeuroPace).
OBSERVATIONS A 17-year-old female underwent placement of an RNS device for drug-resistant epilepsy in the setting of LGS. Five months after
device placement, the patient began experiencing intermittent slurred speech, fatigue, and muscle weakness. Initially, the symptoms were attributed to
increased seizure activity and/or medication side effects. However, despite changing medications and RNS settings, no improvements occurred. Her
antiacetylcholine receptor antibodies measured 62.50 nmol/L, consistent with a diagnosis of MG. The patient was then prescribed pyridostigmine and
underwent a thymectomy, which alleviated most of her symptoms.
LESSONS The authors share the cautionary tale of a case of MG in a pediatric patient who was treated with RNS for intractable epilepsy associated
with LGS. Although slurred speech, fatigue, muscle weakness, and other symptoms might stem from increased seizure activity and/or medication side
effects, they could also be due to MG development.

KEYWORDS myasthenia gravis; responsive neurostimulation; Lennox-Gastaut syndrome; epilepsy
Autoimmune myasthenia gravis (MG) is a neuromuscular disorder typified by impaired transmission of nerve impulses to muscles
due to antibody-mediated blockade and the destruction of postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.1 The age at onset of MG
varies from childhood to late adulthood, with disease peaks in younger adult women and older men.2 Symptoms of MG include ptosis,
double vision, fatigue, muscle weakness, and breathing difficulties.
Medical therapies for MG include acetylcholinesterase inhibitors,
corticosteroids, and immunosuppressants, as well as intravenous
immunoglobulin. Surgical treatment (thymectomy) is an option in cases
of MG with thymoma. Treatments decrease or alleviate symptoms by
increasing the amount of acetylcholine in the synapse and limiting the
autoimmune reaction produced by suppressing the host’s immune
system. Morbidity in MG mostly results from intermittent muscle weakness leading to aspiration pneumonia. Medical therapies have significantly helped in the treatment of MG; approximately 50 years ago, the
mortality rate for MG was approximately 50% to 80%, but it has been
substantially reduced to approximately 4.47%.3
There appears to be an association between MG and epilepsy,
but there is ongoing debate about the strength of this association
and the underlying mechanism. One population study of more than
2 million people reported a 0.4% prevalence of epilepsy in patients
with comorbid MG, whereas a smaller cohort study reported a
cooccurrence rate of 2.9%.4,5 In a similar vein, accumulating data
support an autoimmune basis in patients with antiepileptic drugresistant seizures.6

This patient developed intractable epilepsy in childhood, her condition having failed to respond to 12 antiseizure medications. Despite a plethora of available treatment options for epilepsy, a large
number of patients continue to have seizures.7 For these patients
with intractable epilepsy, surgery is an option and should be considered early in the treatment course, typically after two medications
have failed. Resective surgery boasts the highest cure rate, but its
feasibility can be compromised when there is a challenge in pinpointing epileptic foci or when these foci are located within eloquent
cortex. Historically, concurrent severe psychiatric illness or severe
medical comorbidities have precluded surgery. Currently, many surgical options are available and are not limited to resections. When
surgery is contraindicated, neuromodulation therapies such as responsive neurostimulation (RNS) can be utilized to detect and stop
seizures. The therapeutic effects of RNS are mediated through an
inhibitory polarization caused by transmembrane currents generated
by the applied pulse along selected contacts of either cortical or
depth leads.8 Furthermore, data show that RNS implantation has a
favorable safety profile for pediatric patients. One literature review
revealed that in 49 pediatric patients, no neurological deficits or intracranial hematomas were observed after RNS device implantation.9 We report the case of a pediatric patient with new-onset MG
after RNS who also presented with drug-resistant epilepsy, LennoxGastaut syndrome, and autism.
Illustrative Case
A 17-year-old female presented with intractable Lennox-Gastaut
syndrome (LGS). Her seizure semiology consisted of atonic, generalized tonic-clonic, myoclonic, and atypical absence seizures. The

patient first began having seizures at 5 years old. She was the
product of a full-term pregnancy. Consistent with her diagnosis of
LGS, this patient experienced motor and language-related developmental delays. Genetic testing revealed a 16p11.2 microdeletion,
which is linked to neurodevelopmental diseases, including autism
spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, and epilepsy, among others.10
Delays were noted in this patient at 2 years old. She was not diagnosed with autism until age 8. Prior to RNS, her IQ dropped from the
normal range (100) to a range consistent with borderline intellectual
functioning. Her longest seizure-free interval before RNS implantation
was 12 hours at age 15. Her family history was significant for chromosomal abnormality in her brother with monosomy, who had a few seizures until he was 12 years old.
The patient had tried many antiseizure medications, including zonisamide, ethosuximide, topiramate, levetiracetam, clobazam, rufinamide,
lacosamide, cannabidiol, perampanel, and felbamate, without adequate
control of her disabling seizures. She was currently on clonazepam and
lamotrigine, as well as fluoxetine for autism and obsessive-compulsive
disorder. In 2021, video electroencephalography (EEG) showed generalized spike and wave with a hint of onset from the left hemisphere.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed possible hemosiderin
deposition in the right frontal region, and positron emission tomography
was normal. She underwent placement of bilateral stereo EEG, capturing four seizures with bifrontal onset.
The patient then underwent RNS device implantation to treat her
intractable epilepsy, with bilateral placement of depth electrodes in
the centromedian nuclei of the thalamus. She has had a 95% decrease in clinical events as reported by her parents since RNS device placement, decreasing from two seizures per day to one every
other month.
Five months postRNS implantation, she developed leg weakness
(leading to an inability to stand), confusion, fatigue, daily headaches,
and intermittent slurred speech. Initially, this was thought to be
due to drug interactions or toxicity, as her RNS recordings did
not demonstrate any abnormalities (Fig. 1). She was taking clonazepam, felbamate, lamotrigine, and fluoxetine. Although her
levels were not elevated, her felbamate dosage was reduced to
investigate whether it was the cause of her new symptoms. A
month later, at her next visit, poor oxygen saturation and swallowing issues were noted. Drug toxicity was still suspected.
Given that the evidence disfavored felbamate as the likely etiology, her lamotrigine dosage was then lowered, but the symptoms persisted. Certain symptoms, such as falls, were initially
suspected to be seizures because of their similar semiology,
yet no corresponding activity was detected on the RNS recordings. Six months after the onset of her initial symptoms, the patient started to experience a worsening condition with more
pronounced slurred speech, the emergence of dysphagia, an

inability to dress herself due to muscle weakness, and forgetfulness. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest, blood
work, and an acetylcholine receptor antibody test were ordered to ascertain the underlying cause of these more severe symptoms.
Blood work was negative for Lyme disease and thyroid abnormalities, but her acetylcholine receptor binding antibodies were measured at 62.50 nmol/L, consistent with MG (normal # 0.02 nmol/L).
A CT scan of the chest demonstrated a thymoma (Fig. 2). The prescription of pyridostigmine initially resulted in a significant alleviation
of her symptoms. Since the symptoms did not completely resolve,
she underwent a thymectomy and received intravenous immunoglobulin treatment. After these interventions, the patient’s symptoms have become nearly nonexistent. Now, she experiences reduced
muscle weakness, swallowing problems, slurred speech, fatigue, and
forgetfulness. She continues to receive monthly intravenous immunoglobulin, along with felbamate and lamotrigine, and her seizures continue to be well-controlled with the RNS settings shown in Fig. 3.
Patient Informed Consent
The necessary patient informed consent was obtained in this
study.
Discussion
Observations
To our knowledge, this is the first pediatric patient with intractable
epilepsy, autism, and LGS who presented with MG after RNS device
implantation. Given her medical history and comorbidities, this patient
is on many medications. However, our group was especially concerned with drug toxicity stemming from felbamate and lamotrigine.
Both medications are frequently used to treat epilepsy in patients with
LGS. Felbamate has been reported to cause generalized weakness
and lethargy, making it suspect in causing our patient’s symptoms
originally.11 Similarly, lamotrigine has been shown to cause headaches
and weakness as adverse reactions.12 Considering the elevated acetylcholine receptor binding antibodies in this patient and the alleviation
of her symptoms after pyridostigmine administration, thymectomy, and
intravenous immunoglobulin treatment, an autoimmune condition, specifically MG, seems to be the most likely underlying cause.

Although there is a report in which MG developed in a patient
25 months after RNS device implantation, the etiology was unknown.13
It is extremely unlikely that RNS implantation led to MG in that patient;
RNS tracks and prevents seizure activity and would therefore have no
association with an autoimmune condition like MG. Plus, there have
been no other reports of such an occurrence.
MG can develop as a consequence of a constellation of conditions and medications, rather than being solely attributed to one ailment. Many reports have also indicated that MG can be triggered
and worsened by infections, such as coronavirus disease 2019
(COVID-19), a particularly prevalent and noteworthy virus today.
Not only have many neurological complications been described in
the medical literature after COVID-19 infection, but the worsening of
preexisting MG and the development of new-onset MG have specifically been described several times.14–16
Antiepileptic drugs, which our patient had been taking for most
of her life, have not been reported to induce de novo MG or exacerbate it, but drug classes such as immune checkpoint inhibitors,
d-penicillamines, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and interferons have been
implicated in the development of this autoimmune reaction.17 Our patient was not treated with any of these drug classes, but we did suspect that her initial weakness stemmed from toxicity due to one or
more of her antiepileptic medications. This is why both her felbamate
and lamotrigine doses were decreased. For reasons previously mentioned, RNS was never suspected to be the cause of any of her MG
symptoms.

thymoma.

Associations have been made between MG and central nervous
system functions for more than 100 years.18 In patients with MG,
an elevated incidence of epilepsy has been noted, as well as psychiatric disorders and multiple sclerosis.18 Two hypotheses for how

MG and epilepsy are related have been described.5 First, respiratory muscle weakness in MG patients may lead to hypoventilation,
hypoxia, and sleep apnea, resulting in EEG changes such as mild
diffuse slowing.17 Second, there are certain antibodies that can increase the likelihood of seizures and are related to autoimmune diseases such as MG.19,20 One of these epileptogenic antibodies is
anti-NMDAR. It causes a decrease in the density of the NMDAR,
which impairs its synaptic function. Given the autoimmune nature of
MG, it could potentially be associated with other autoimmune diseases and epileptogenic antibodies such as NMDAR that are found
in a subset of seizure disorders. For our patient, it is unlikely that
her intractable epilepsy and LGS directly precipitated MG, as the
two hypotheses describe how MG leads to epilepsy. However, it is
less surprising that MG and epilepsy occurred in the same patient
given population data and the possible association that exists.
Lessons
This illustrative case is not without limitations. First and perhaps
most evidently, one cannot draw statistically significant conclusions
from a sample size of one patient. Therefore, this illustrative case is
intended to serve as a cautionary tale for other clinicians caring for
patients with one or more of the conditions and/or medications described. Although drug toxicity, drug interactions, or increased seizure
activity may seem like common culprits in symptoms of fatigue, muscle weakness, and headaches, it can also be something rarer, such
as MG. Second, we are still not certain what led to the onset of MG
in our patient. Last, although a thymectomy, intravenous immunoglobulin, and pyridostigmine administration led to an improvement in our
patient’s MG symptoms, other medications and treatment options exist for pediatric patients, such as steroids, immunosuppressants, and
plasmapheresis. We hope that future studies will further explore the
timeline of drug toxicity to the onset of MG, as well as any potential
link between conditions such as LGS and the development of MG or
other autoimmune conditions.
